title: From Detection to Understanding: TAR and TAR-Bench for Multi-Task Traffic Anomaly Reasoning
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: A single annotated example shows how one input is paired with multiple complementary reasoning tasks organized into groups.
layout: Top two video frames with timeline bar, below three colored task-group columns
description: The top of the figure shows two CCTV video frames of a multi-lane road, timestamped 00:05.6 and 00:07.2. They show a silver sedan turning across the lanes and then colliding with an SUV. Below them is a gray timeline bar running from 00:00 to 00:12, with a green segment marking the critical anomaly interval. Three columns sit under the timeline, each topped by a colored rule: green for Question Answering, blue for Temporal Reasoning, purple for Scene Understanding. Each column lists its task abbreviations, such as BCQ, MCQ, TL, TD, CL, SD and VS. Each also has a tinted card with one example Q, A and a grayed-out rationale R. The eye goes first to the large video frames, then down to the three color-coded cards.
caption: TAR and TAR-Bench provide multi-task reasoning annotations for traffic videos. Each clip is paired with questions, answers, and supporting reasoning traces for ten tasks in three groups: Question Answering, Temporal Reasoning, and Scene Understanding.
abstract: Detecting a traffic anomaly does not establish whether a video-language model can explain what happened, localize it in time, or identify its causes. We introduce TAR (Traffic Anomaly Reasoning) and TAR-Bench, paired resources for training and evaluating these complementary capabilities across 10 tasks spanning question answering, temporal reasoning, and scene understanding. TAR contains 44,040 automatically generated annotations with chain-of-thought traces for 3,670 CCTV videos from eight public datasets. TAR-Bench provides 960 human-curated annotations for 80 held-out clips from 17 public YouTube videos. Evaluation of eleven vision-language models and analysis of fine-tuned outputs reveal temporal, causal, and descriptive errors not captured by closed-form question-answering accuracy. Training on all 10 tasks raises mean benchmark scores from 34.3 to 55.7 for Cosmos-Reason2-8B and from 30.9 to 53.9 for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. These results support joint training across complementary tasks, while highlighting persistent limitations in temporal precision and causal attribution. TAR and TAR-Bench serve as the official training and in-domain evaluation resources for AI City Challenge 2026 Track~3. The dataset is available under CC-BY-4.0 at https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/PhysicalAI-Traffic-Anomaly-Reasoning.
